summary: DNSSEC relies on cryptographic algorithms that must interoperate. This document sets out the process for updating recommendations on which algorithms implementations should support. It obsoletes RFC 8624 and updates RFC 9157.

plainLanguage.summary: As some lock types become weak, someone has to update the list of recommended locks. This explains how that list is kept up to date.

questions: where is the dnssec algorithm list kept
subtitle: DNSSEC algorithm advice moves out of a fixed RFC and into the IANA registries, so it can change without a new document.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC software has to agree on which cryptographic algorithms to support, but putting that list in an RFC made it slow to update as algorithms age.
tldr.mechanism: The canonical list moves from RFC 8624 into new columns of the IANA DNS Security Algorithm Numbers and Digest Algorithms registries, and rules say how entries may be added or changed.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9904 obsoletes RFC 8624 and updates RFC 9157, and it does not change any algorithm's recommendation level.

today: RFC 9904 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2025. It obsoletes RFC 8624 and updates RFC 9157, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Moving the List to IANA
sections.content:
DNSSEC authenticates DNS data, and its signing algorithms are defined in many RFCs. To make sure at least one algorithm is supported everywhere, RFC 8624 defined a set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms. RFC 9904 moves the canonical status of those algorithms from RFC 8624 to the IANA DNSSEC algorithm registries, so the requirements are easier to read and to update. It uses the same approach as the TLS Cipher Suites registry.

It also folds in the revised IANA considerations from RFC 9157 and adds advice for operators on which algorithms to deploy, whatever implementations support. Deployment of aging algorithms is expected to shrink before implementations stop supporting them.

The document does not change the MUST, MAY or RECOMMENDED status of any algorithm listed in RFC 8624. That is left to future documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of safe locks moves from a printed book to a notice board anyone can check, and nobody has been added or removed yet.

sections.title: How Requirement Levels Are Meant to Change
sections.content:
Recommendations are expected to change as algorithms are attacked or new ones appear. The RFC says deprecation should be gradual: unless there are strong security reasons, an algorithm should drop from MUST to NOT RECOMMENDED or MAY rather than straight to MUST NOT. A new algorithm should first be RECOMMENDED rather than MUST.

An unknown DNSKEY algorithm makes a zone look insecure, so algorithms at NOT RECOMMENDED or lower should not be used by authoritative servers and signers to create new DNSKEYs. Once an algorithm is rarely deployed it can become MUST NOT, so that recursive resolvers can drop validation support for it. Validating resolvers are encouraged to keep support for everything not marked MUST NOT.
sections.plainLanguage: When a lock gets old, you first stop buying it, and only much later stop keeping the key, so nobody gets locked out suddenly.

sections.title: The New Registry Columns
sections.content:
Each of the two registries gets four new columns. In the DNS Security Algorithm Numbers registry they are Use for DNSSEC Signing, Use for DNSSEC Validation, Implement for DNSSEC Signing and Implement for DNSSEC Validation. In the Digest Algorithms registry they are the same, with Delegation replacing Signing. The "Use for" columns say what to deploy, and the "Implement for" columns say what software should support.

The "Use for" columns may hold MAY, RECOMMENDED, MUST NOT or NOT RECOMMENDED. The "Implement for" columns may also hold MUST. The initial "Implement for" values are transcribed from RFC 8624, and the "Use for" values are copied from them, except that a MUST becomes RECOMMENDED.

New entries with the value MAY follow Specification Required. Any other value, or changing an existing value, needs Standards Action. An entry that is not RECOMMENDED is not necessarily flawed; it may simply lack IETF consensus review or have limited applicability.
sections.plainLanguage: Each algorithm gets four boxes to tick: should I use it, and should I build it, for signing and for checking.

sections.title: Initial Values
sections.content:
Table 2 of the RFC fills in the algorithm registry. Algorithms 1 (RSAMD5), 3 (DSA) and 6 (DSA-NSEC3-SHA1) are MUST NOT in all four columns. Algorithms 5 (RSASHA1), 7 (RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1) and 10 (RSASHA512) are NOT RECOMMENDED for signing but still RECOMMENDED for validation use, with validators told to implement them (MUST). Algorithms 8 (RSASHA256) and 13 (ECDSAP256SHA256) are RECOMMENDED for use and MUST be implemented, and 15 (ED25519) is RECOMMENDED throughout.

Table 3 does the same for digests. Digest 2 (SHA-256) is RECOMMENDED for use and MUST be implemented. Digest 1 (SHA-1) is MUST NOT for delegation but still a MUST for validators to implement. When several algorithms are RECOMMENDED, operators choose by local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The starting list marks some old locks as banned, some as fine to check but not to buy, and a few modern ones as the best choice.

sections.title: Security and Operational Notes
sections.content:
The algorithms marked MUST or RECOMMENDED to implement are, according to the RFC, not known to be broken, but future documents are expected to track best practice. Retiring an algorithm too soon would turn a zone signed with it into the equivalent of an unsigned zone, so deprecation must be careful and ideally slow.

Algorithm rollover in a live zone is complex; the RFC points to RFC 6781 and RFC 7583. For DS digest algorithms, upgrading the digest at the same time as rolling to a new Key Signing Key causes validation failures, so operators MUST upgrade the DS algorithm first.

IANA has added the columns, changed the registration procedure to Standards Action or Specification Required, added the explanatory notes and listed this document as a reference. In the Digest Algorithms registry it also reserved values 128 to 252, marked 253 and 254 Reserved for Private Use and removed the Status column.
sections.plainLanguage: Switching locks has to be done in the right order, or people will be shut out of their own house.
